title: Mind and memory
goals: Compress ideas with participle clauses (Having finished…, Not knowing…, Built in 1900…) and choose the form that fits the meaning.
Avoid dangling participles: use the same subject or a fixed connector (Generally speaking, Judging by…).
Use reduced relative clauses with participles (people waiting…, data collected…) and to + infinitive (the first to arrive).
Talk about psychology and memory with precise vocabulary (recall, vivid, trigger, cognitive, retain).
Master memory collocations and idioms (on the tip of my tongue, ring a bell, draw a blank).
Write dense, well-connected texts in a formal register.

learn.title: Participle clauses: forms and connectors
learn.html:
A participle clause replaces a subordinate clause (of time, cause, condition…) and compresses it: As she was walking home, she… → Walking home, she…. It is a typical feature of written and formal English: it gives density and avoids repeating the subject and the conjunction. In Spanish it resembles the gerund and the past participle, but English is much more systematic.

FormMeaningExample
V-ing (active)Simultaneous or immediately preceding action; causeOpening the drawer, she found the letter.
Having + V-ed (perfect active)Action completed BEFORE the main clause; causeHaving read the report, she called her lawyer.
V-ed / past participle (passive)Passive meaning, without beingBuilt in 1900, the house needs repairs.
Being + V-ed / Having been + V-edExplicit passive (ongoing / earlier)Having been warned twice, he ignored us.
Not + participleNegative: not goes in frontNot knowing the way, we asked for help.

With a conjunction: the conjunction is often kept to clarify the relationship: after / before / while / since / on / upon / once / when + V-ing (After leaving school, he…; Upon arriving, please…) and although / if / unless / when / once + V-ed (Although tired, she…; Unless treated, the infection spreads).

V-ing or Having V-ed: if the actions are almost simultaneous or follow each other immediately, V-ing is enough (Turning the key, he opened the door). If there is a clear gap between them or the first is a previous state, use Having (Having lived abroad for ten years, she…). State verbs (know, be, have) usually prefer Being or Having been/known, depending on the meaning.

watch.wrong: Having finish the exam, we left.
watch.right: Having finished the exam, we left.
watch.why: Having + past participle (finished), not the base form.

watch.wrong: Not having knew the answer, she guessed.
watch.right: Not knowing the answer, she guessed.
watch.why: Not goes in front and the verb takes the participle (knowing / having known).

watch.wrong: Be tired after the flight, he slept at once.
watch.right: Being tired after the flight, he slept at once.
watch.why: Being is needed (or it is omitted): the bare base verb does not work as a clause.

watch.wrong: Knowing her for years, I could tell she was lying.
watch.right: Having known her for years, I could tell she was lying.
watch.why: A state that had been going on before requires Having known.

learn.title: What the clause means: time, cause, condition, contrast
learn.html:
The participle clause does not say by itself whether it expresses time, cause or condition: the reader infers it from context. That ambiguity is what must be handled with care.

RelationshipExampleEquivalent to
Sequence / timeHaving checked the figures, she signed.After she had checked…
CauseNot wanting to wake anyone, he left quietly.Because he didn't want…
ConditionUsed properly, the technique improves recall.If it is used properly…
Contrast (with conjunction)Although exhausted, she kept studying.Although she was exhausted…
Result / consequenceThe storm hit at dawn, causing power cuts across the region.…and it caused…
Simultaneous descriptionShe sat by the window, staring at the rain.…and she stared…

Position: at the start (time or cause frame; takes a comma), at the end (result or accompaniment), or inserted between commas (The proposal, having been rejected twice, was shelved). In spoken register a full clause is much more natural (Because I didn't know the way, I asked); in an essay, a report or a literary narrative the participle sounds more polished.

Nuance: a final -ing after a comma = result or accompaniment (…causing delays); without it, the reading changes. Born in Leeds, she… (= as she was born in Leeds; being is omitted): notice we use born, not being born, although both are possible.

watch.wrong: Being born in Lima, she speaks with a Peruvian accent.
watch.right: Born in Lima, she speaks with a Peruvian accent.
watch.why: With a place or date of birth, born is preferred, without being.

watch.wrong: Having arrived late, the meeting had already started.
watch.right: Having arrived late, we found that the meeting had already started.
watch.why: The subject of the participle clause must be the subject of the main clause.

watch.wrong: Using the new software, the problem was solved.
watch.right: Using the new software, we solved the problem.
watch.why: Whoever uses the software is a person; the passive breaks the subject relationship.

watch.wrong: Using properly, the tool is safe.
watch.right: Used properly, the tool is safe.
watch.why: Passive meaning: the tool IS used, which is why it takes the past participle.

learn.title: Same subject and dangling participles
learn.html:
Golden rule: the implied subject of the participle clause is the subject of the main clause. If they do not match, we have a dangling participle: Walking down the street, a bicycle almost hit me suggests that the bicycle was walking. It is a very common error, even among native speakers, but it is penalised in formal writing.

IncorrectCorrection
Reading the article, the argument seemed weak.Reading the article, I found the argument weak.
Surprised by the results, the experiment was repeated.Surprised by the results, the team repeated the experiment.
Having been warned, the storm didn't scare us.Having been warned, we weren't scared by the storm.

Accepted exceptions: fixed expressions that work as connectors and do not require the same subject: Generally speaking, Strictly speaking, Judging by…, Considering…, Given that…, Taking everything into account, Speaking of which, Weather permitting, All things considered.

Own subject (absolute clause): if you want a different subject, make it explicit: The deadline being so close, we skipped the meeting; Her phone ringing, she left the room; Weather permitting, the match will go ahead. It is a very formal and literary register; with with it sounds more modern: With the deadline so close, we skipped the meeting.

Revision strategy: after the comma, ask yourself «who is doing the action of the clause?» and check that it is the word the main clause begins with.

watch.wrong: Walking down the street, a bicycle almost hit me.
watch.right: Walking down the street, I was almost hit by a bicycle.
watch.why: The subject of walking must be 'I', not 'a bicycle'.

watch.wrong: Having finished the exam, the teacher collected the papers.
watch.right: Having finished the exam, the students handed in their papers.
watch.why: Same subject for both actions: whoever finished the exam are the students.

watch.wrong: Being the nice day, we went to the park.
watch.right: The day being nice, we went to the park.
watch.why: With its own subject, it is made explicit (absolute clause); also: It being a nice day.

watch.wrong: Having a lot of work, the weekend was spent in the office.
watch.right: Having a lot of work, I spent the weekend in the office.
watch.why: The person who has the work is a person, not the weekend.

learn.title: Reduced relative clauses with participles
learn.html:
Relative clauses with who / which / that + verb can be reduced to a participle when the relative pronoun is the subject of the clause. It is the same condensing device as participle clauses, but in post-noun position.

Full relative clauseReducedRule
The people who are waiting outside…The people waiting outside…Active: V-ing
The data that was collected last year…The data collected last year…Passive: V-ed
Anyone who wants to apply…Anyone wanting to apply…Present / habitual: V-ing
The first student who arrived…The first student to arrive…After first/last/only/superlative: to + infinitive
Memories which have been triggered by smell…Memories triggered by smell…The auxiliary have been is omitted

Limits: you cannot reduce a relative clause whose relative pronoun is the object and keeps its own subject (the book that I borrowed: there is no participle reduction that keeps «I»). Nor can you do so with static verbs when meaning is lost (the man who owns the shop → the man owning the shop is possible but unnatural; prefer the shop's owner). A reduced clause with -ing expresses a habitual or ongoing action; it does not serve for completed one-off actions (the man who arrived yesterday, not the man arriving yesterday).

In non-defining clauses: they are used between commas and sound formal: My brother, working in Madrid, rarely visits. They are most easily recognised in headlines and academic summaries: Participants given the drug performed better.

watch.wrong: The researchers interviewing on the radio yesterday were nervous.
watch.right: The researchers interviewed on the radio yesterday were nervous.

watch.wrong: The man sat opposite me was reading.
watch.right: The man sitting opposite me was reading.

watch.wrong: The people lived next door are friendly.
watch.right: The people living next door are friendly.

watch.wrong: The first person arriving gets a prize.
watch.right: The first person to arrive gets a prize.

learn.title: Connecting ideas and writing densely
learn.html:
• Having said that, … / That said, … — introduce a counterpoint without breaking the formal tone.
  • Given that … / Considering that … — justify an idea with a premise.
  • Generally / Broadly / Strictly speaking, … — qualify the scope of the statement (they do not require the same subject).
  • Judging by … / Taking everything into account, … — support a conclusion with evidence.
  • Put simply, … / In other words, … — restate clearly.
  • Seen in this light, … / Viewed from this angle, … — introduce an interpretation.
  • Whereas / While + full clause — contrast two facts; , thereby + V-ing — mark a result: She automated the process, thereby saving hours.
  • Not only … but also … and V-ing, which — add weighty information: The study is small, which limits its conclusions.

Tip: in a dense paragraph, alternate long sentences with participles and short concluding sentences. Avoid chaining more than two participle clauses in a row.

practice.title: Form of the participle

answers: Built

answers: Being

answers: reading
having read
items.explain: After after: V-ing or having + past participle.

Having lost her keys, Sara could not get in.

practice.title: Choose the form or the meaning

items.explain: First he received the offer, then he decided: Having received.

items.prompt: ___ by the noise, the baby started to cry.
items.explain: Passive: woken (the baby is woken up).

options: Opening the door, he turned the key.
Having turned the key, he opened the door.
Turning the key, he opened the door.
items.explain: Having + past participle marks an earlier action.

items.prompt: ___ wanting to disturb them, I left quietly.
items.explain: In the negative, Not goes before the participle.

items.prompt: ___ her for years, I could tell she was lying.
items.explain: A long-lasting earlier state: Having known.

items.prompt: ___ properly, the technique can improve recall.
items.explain: Passive-conditional meaning: Used (= if it is used).

items.prompt: On ___ the results, the team realised the experiment had failed.
items.explain: On + V-ing = upon + gerund (e.g. «on seeing» ≈ «upon seeing»).

items.prompt: Which one is INCORRECT?
options: Having finished the exam, he relaxed.
items.explain: A simple past participle ('Finished') has a passive meaning; here Having finished is needed.

items.prompt: The people ___ (wait) outside are from the press.
answers: waiting
items.explain: Reduced active relative: V-ing.

items.prompt: The data ___ (collect) last year was incomplete.
answers: collected
items.explain: Reduced passive relative: V-ed.

items.prompt: Anyone ___ to join the study should email us.
items.explain: Anyone wanting to join = anyone who wants to join.

items.prompt: The researchers interviewing on the radio yesterday were nervous.
answers: The researchers interviewed on the radio yesterday were nervous.

items.prompt: The first person ___ (arrive) will get a prize.
answers: to arrive

items.prompt: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced with a participle while keeping the subject 'I'?
options: The students who were chosen for the trial
The book that I borrowed from you
The people who live next door
items.explain: The relative is the object and the clause keeps its own subject (I).

items.prompt: Students ___ (suffer) from stress often struggle to retain information.
answers: suffering
items.explain: Habitual active relative: V-ing.

items.prompt: Los pacientes tratados con este método mejoraron.
answers: Patients treated with this method improved.
The patients treated with this method improved.
Patients treated with this method got better.
The patients treated with this method got better.
items.explain: Past participle for passive meaning: treated.

items.prompt: Surprising by the results, the team repeated the experiment.

items.explain: Passive meaning: surprised.

items.prompt: I can't ___ where I parked the car.
answers: recall
remember

answers: vivid

items.prompt: The smell of baking bread was a ___ for childhood memories.

consolidate
process
store

items.prompt: A ___ study measures attention, memory and problem-solving.

items.prompt: Over time, even the most intense emotions ___.
answers: fade

items.prompt: Which word means 'to bring back something stored in memory'?

items.prompt: A wave of ___ made her scroll through old photos for hours.
answers: nostalgia

items.prompt: His name is on the tip of my ___, but I can't say it.

write.prompt: Write an essay of 250 to 350 words titled «Why we remember what we remember»: explain why memory is not a faithful archive, give one concrete example (personal or from a study) and propose two tips for remembering better. Use at least five varied participle clauses and two reduced relative clauses.
checklist: Between 250 and 350 words, with introduction, development and conclusion
At least 5 participle clauses (V-ing, Having V-ed, V-ed, Not V-ing)
Same subject in the participle clause and the main clause (no dangling participles)
2 reduced relative clauses (people waiting…, data collected…)
Vocabulary: recall, retain, vivid, trigger, cognitive, fade
Varied linkers (Having said that, Given that, Whereas…)
Mix of long and short sentences; formal register
write.model:
Why we remember what we remember

We tend to think of memory as an archive, a place where experiences are stored intact and retrieved whenever we need them. Cognitive psychology suggests otherwise. Having studied recall for decades, researchers now agree that memory is not a faithful record but a reconstruction, rebuilt each time we call something to mind.

A famous experiment illustrates the point. Shown a film of a car accident, participants were later asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other. Those given the verb "smashed" estimated higher speeds, and many even recalled seeing broken glass that was never there. Whereas the original event was identical for everyone, the wording of a single question altered what people remembered. Given that we reconstruct the past in the present, it is hardly surprising that our recollections are shaped by what we know, feel and expect today.

My own experience confirms this. Having heard my family tell the story of my fifth birthday so often, I can now recall it in vivid detail, yet my parents insist that I was not even there, because I was ill in bed. Not realising it, I had absorbed their account and turned it into a memory of my own.

Why, then, do some memories survive while others fade? Events accompanied by strong emotion are retained better, as are those repeated at intervals. Having said that, repetition can also distort, as the birthday story shows. People trying to remember more effectively might therefore follow two simple tips. First, test yourself rather than simply rereading notes, since effort strengthens retrieval. Second, link new information to a trigger, such as a place or a smell, so that your brain can find the path back to it later.

Memory, in short, is less a library than a storyteller. Accepting this need not make us distrust ourselves; knowing how it works, we can learn to use it more wisely.

write.prompt: In 250 to 350 words, write a narrative or blog post about a very vivid memory (a smell, a song, a place) that takes you back to the past. Describe the scene, what triggers it and how it has changed over time. Use participles to link the actions and collocations such as ring a bell, fade, be etched in my memory.
checklist: At least 4 participle clauses (time, cause, description)
At least 3 memory collocations or idioms
write.model:
Every autumn, the smell of woodsmoke stops me in my tracks. Walking down a street in the city last week, I caught it on the wind, and in an instant I was eight years old again, standing in my grandfather's garden.

The scene is etched in my memory. Wearing a coat two sizes too big, I am watching him burn dry leaves in an old metal barrel. Smoke curls upward, tinged with orange by the setting sun, and the whole garden smells of apples and damp earth. Sitting on an upturned crate, my grandfather hums a tune I could never name, and I remember the warmth of the fire on my cheeks. Having finished his work, he hands me a roasted chestnut, too hot to hold, and laughs as I juggle it between my palms.

What triggers the memory is not only the smell, but a particular quality of light, thin and golden, that I only see in late October. Whenever it appears, the tune starts to ring a bell, although I still cannot say where I heard it. Perhaps it was never a real song, just one he made up.

Over the years the memory has changed. Some details have started to fade: I can no longer picture the colour of the gate, and I am not sure whether the crate was blue or green. Others, strangely, have grown sharper. Having retold the story to my children, I have probably added things that never happened, such as the chestnut, which my mother insists was a biscuit.

Yet I do not mind. Memories like this one do not need to be accurate to be valuable. Gone for twenty years, my grandfather still visits me every autumn, carried on a thread of smoke. And perhaps that is what remembering really is: not an exact copy of the past, but a way of keeping those we love close, even as the details slip away.

reading.title: The Unreliable Archive
reading.intro: Read the article about how memory really works and answer the questions.
paragraphs: Most of us instinctively treat memory as an archive: experiences, once stored, are filed away and can be pulled out whenever we need them. Decades of research, however, point in a rather different direction. Far from being a faithful recording, memory is a reconstruction, rebuilt each time we recall an event and therefore open to quiet, almost imperceptible revision.

One of the best-known demonstrations dates from the 1970s. Shown footage of a minor car accident, volunteers were asked how fast the vehicles had been travelling when they either "hit" or "smashed into" each other. Those given the more dramatic verb gave higher estimates and, a week later, many of them "remembered" broken glass that had never appeared on screen. Having been nudged by a single word, their memories had rewritten themselves without anyone noticing.

Emotion complicates the picture further. People who lived through a landmark event, such as a national tragedy, often describe their recollections as vivid, almost photographic. Yet studies tracking the same individuals over several years show that the details drift considerably, while confidence in them remains stubbornly high. Intense feelings seem to strengthen the sense of certainty rather than the accuracy of what is retained. The brain, having flagged the moment as important, stamps it with a feeling of authenticity that is surprisingly easy to mistake for proof.

None of this means that memory is useless. Quite the opposite: a system designed to extract the gist of experience, rather than to preserve every detail, serves us remarkably well most of the time. Researchers working in this field tend to stress that forgetting is not a malfunction but a feature, allowing the mind to discard clutter and focus on patterns. The difficulty arises when we confuse the two roles and rely on recollection in situations demanding precision, such as eyewitness testimony.

What, then, can be done? The most robust finding in the literature is also the least glamorous. Information retrieved repeatedly is retained far better than information simply reread, which is why a student testing herself on yesterday's notes will outperform one who highlights the same pages for an hour. Spacing matters too: sessions spread over several days beat a single marathon, provided each one demands real effort. Sleep, often sacrificed first when deadlines loom, plays a decisive role in consolidating what has been learnt. Cut short, it leaves fragile traces that fade within days.

There is also a humbler lesson. Knowing that recollections are reconstructed should make us more charitable when two people remember the same argument differently. Neither is necessarily lying; both may be sincerely describing a version assembled from fragments, shaped by mood, hindsight and the stories told since. Seen this way, a disagreement about the past stops being a contest about who is right and becomes an invitation to compare reconstructions, which is, after all, what any good historian does.

Memoirists have understood this for centuries. Writing about her childhood, one novelist admitted that the scenes she described felt "more true than the facts", having been polished by decades of retelling. Perhaps the wisest attitude is a flexible one: to treat our most cherished memories with affection, and our certainty about them with a measure of scepticism.

listening.title: Why can't I remember names?
listening.intro: Listen to an extract from a radio programme. You can play it again.

lines.text: Welcome back to Brain Matters. Today we're tackling a question that has probably embarrassed every one of us at a party: why can't I remember that person's name?
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it's one of the most common complaints I hear, and in most cases there's nothing wrong with your memory at all.
That's a relief. So what's going on?

Well, names are arbitrary. A face comes with a rich web of associations, whereas a name is just a label, so there's very little for the brain to hook it onto. Having heard a name once, most people never rehearse it.
Right, we're busy thinking about what to say next instead of listening.
Exactly. The information never gets properly encoded, so you can't retrieve what was never stored.
Hi, can I jump in? My problem's the opposite. I remember everything, including things I'd rather forget, like an embarrassing speech I gave ten years ago.
Ha, that's very common too. Emotionally charged events tend to be vivid, and the memory gets replayed every time something triggers it. Replaying it, you actually strengthen the trace.
So the more I cringe, the more I remember?
More or less. A trick that helps is to describe the event in a different tone. Tell it as a funny story. Told with a bit of distance, the memory loses its sting.
And for the rest of us, any quick tips for names?
Repeat the name immediately, use it in the conversation, and link it to something: a rhyme, an image, whatever sticks. Don't just say 'nice to meet you'. Say 'nice to meet you, Daniel'.
And if it's on the tip of my tongue? Should I keep struggling?
Better to move on. Distracted by something else, your brain often keeps searching in the background, and the word pops up when you stop trying.

tasks.prompt: Tell about a very vivid memory from your childhood and what triggers it.
questions: What is one of your most vivid childhood memories?
What usually triggers it: a smell, a song, a place?
How has the memory changed over the years?
Do you trust it completely? Why, or why not?
tasks.model: One memory that is etched in my mind is my grandmother's kitchen on Sunday mornings. Walking past a bakery, I sometimes catch the smell of sweet bread, and I'm suddenly eight years old again. Having heard the story so many times, I'm no longer sure which details are real and which I've added. Still, the feeling is vivid.
checklist: Use at least two participle clauses
Qualify how reliable the memory is (I'm no longer sure…)

tasks.prompt: Discuss: How reliable is an eyewitness's memory in a trial?

What factors can distort a memory?

Have you ever remembered something differently from someone else?
tasks.model: Generally speaking, eyewitness testimony is persuasive, yet research shows that memories can be reshaped by leading questions. Given that confidence doesn't guarantee accuracy, I think courts should treat it as one piece of evidence among several. Questions asked in a neutral way would help, as would recording statements immediately.

tasks.prompt: Advise a student on how to retain what they study better.
questions: What study habits do you recommend?
Why is rereading less effective than self-testing?
tasks.model: My advice is to test yourself rather than reread. Information retrieved from memory is retained far better. Spread your sessions over several days, and don't sacrifice sleep: having slept well, your brain consolidates what you've learnt. Avoid cramming, which only gives the illusion of knowing.
